title: What is a job task analysis?
description: A job task analysis identifies a job's tasks and the knowledge, skills and abilities each needs. Methods, outputs, and why certification relies on it.
shortAnswer: A job task analysis is a systematic study of a job that identifies the tasks people perform, how often and how critically, and the knowledge, skills and abilities needed to perform each task. Its outputs are a validated task list and linked competency requirements, which become the evidence base for training content, competency frameworks and assessments. Certification schemes for persons and government selection processes treat it as the foundation for valid assessment.
keyTakeaways: A job task analysis identifies tasks, rates their importance or criticality, and links each task to the knowledge, skills and abilities it requires.
Government selection guidance treats job analysis as the foundation for all assessment and selection decisions, and as a source of legal defensibility.
ISO/IEC 17024 certification schemes for persons rest on a job or practice analysis, which is also known as job-task analysis, practice analysis or role delineation study.
Common methods include observation, interviews, work diaries, surveys and facilitated expert panels such as DACUM; most analyses combine a panel with a validation survey.

sections.heading: How is a job task analysis defined?

blocks.text: A job task analysis is defined as a method for identifying the tasks of a job and the competence associated with them. Definitions from government HR policy and from conformity assessment standards agree on that core, and both stress the link between tasks and the knowledge and skills behind them.

The US Office of Personnel Management (OPM), for example, states that a job analysis "identifies the competencies/KSAs directly related to performance on the job. It is a systematic procedure for gathering, documenting, and analyzing information about the content, context, and requirements of the job" ([OPM](https://www.opm.gov/frequently-asked-questions/assessment-policy-faq/job-analysis/what-is-a-job-analysis/)). OPM describes job analysis as "the foundation for all assessment and selection decisions" ([OPM](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/assessment-and-selection/job-analysis/)).

In certification of persons, the vocabulary standard ISO/IEC 17027, as presented by the [International Accreditation Forum](https://iaf.nu/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/03_Certification_Schemes.pdf), defines job analysis as the "method(s) used to identify the tasks and associated competence". Its notes add that "job analysis provides the basis for the validity of any assessments used in issuing credentials" and that other terms for it are "job-task analysis, practice analysis, performance analysis and role-delineation study".

sections.heading: Where is a job task analysis required or expected?

blocks.text: A job task analysis is expected wherever an assessment must be shown to be valid and job related: certification of persons, regulated selection processes and competency-based training systems. Organizations without a formal requirement still use it because it gives training and assessment a defensible basis.

items: **Certification of persons (ISO/IEC 17024):** the Irish National Accreditation Board (INAB) explains that "as part of scheme development, a job or practice analysis is conducted", identifying the tasks for successful performance, the competence required for each task, prerequisites, assessment mechanisms and examination content, and recertification requirements and interval ([INAB](https://www.inab.ie/news-resources/publications/iso-iec-17024-conformity-assessment-general-requirements-for-bodies-operating-certification-of-persons.pdf)). ISO/IEC 17024:2026, published in March 2026, keeps job and practice analysis as a core scheme concept.

**Government selection:** OPM says job analysis data establishes and documents the competencies required for a job, shows the job relatedness of tasks and competencies, and provides "a source of legal defensibility of assessment and selection procedures".
**Competency-based training:** occupational analysis methods such as DACUM are used to build competency-based curricula. See [competency based training](/glossary/competency-based-training).

sections.heading: What methods are used for a job task analysis?

blocks.text: The main methods are observation, interviews, work diaries, surveys and facilitated expert panels. Most rigorous analyses use a panel to draft the task list and a survey of a wider group of job holders to validate and rate it.

blocks.text: DACUM (Developing a Curriculum) is a widely used panel method. The [Center on Education and Training for Employment](https://cete.osu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/CETE-Works_Job-Analysis-Whats-in-a-Job_Transcript.pdf) at The Ohio State University, which runs the DACUM International Training Center, describes it as a method first developed in Canada in the late 1960s and early 1970s, using a panel of usually six to ten expert job holders who describe their duties and tasks to a facilitator, typically over a two-day workshop. The resulting chart serves as the foundation for competency-based training.

sections.heading: What does a job task analysis produce?

blocks.text: A job task analysis produces a validated list of duties and tasks, ratings that show which tasks matter most, and the knowledge, skills and abilities linked to each task. Those outputs feed directly into the competency framework, training design and assessment blueprint.

The full method, including survey design and how ratings translate into training and assessment priorities, is covered in [how to conduct a job task analysis](/guides/how-to-conduct-a-job-task-analysis). The weighted results become an [assessment blueprint](/glossary/assessment-blueprint).

sections.heading: How is a job task analysis different from a training needs analysis?

blocks.text: A job task analysis describes the job: what must be done and what it takes. A [training needs analysis](/glossary/training-needs-analysis) describes the people: how current capability compares with what the job requires. The job task analysis comes first and supplies the standard the needs analysis measures against.

items: **Job task analysis vs competency framework:** the analysis is the evidence; the [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework) is the structured standard built from it.
**Job task analysis vs job description:** a job description summarizes purpose and responsibilities at a high level; a task analysis breaks the work into rated, assessable tasks.

**Job task analysis vs SME interviews alone:** unstructured expert input is a useful source, but without validation across job holders it reflects a few individuals. See [how to capture subject matter expert knowledge](/guides/how-to-capture-subject-matter-expert-knowledge).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry stores task analysis outputs as linked records: tasks connect to the knowledge and skills they need, to the competencies built from them, and to the assessment items that sample them. When a task changes, the affected competencies and assessments can be found rather than rediscovered.

faqs.q: How often should a job task analysis be repeated?
faqs.a: Repeat it when the job changes materially, for example through new technology, regulation or procedures, and on a fixed cycle as a backstop. Certification schemes under ISO/IEC 17024 also use the analysis to set recertification requirements and intervals, so the analysis needs to stay current for the scheme to remain valid.

faqs.q: Who should take part in a job task analysis?
faqs.a: Experienced, currently practicing job holders are the core, supported by supervisors and, where relevant, regulators or quality staff. A validation survey should then reach a broader and representative sample of job holders across locations, shifts and experience levels.

faqs.q: Is job analysis the same as job task analysis?
faqs.a: In practice the terms are used interchangeably. ISO/IEC 17027 lists job-task analysis, practice analysis, performance analysis and role delineation study as other terms for job analysis. Some writers reserve job analysis for broader studies that also cover working conditions and pay.

faqs.q: Do small organizations need a formal job task analysis?
faqs.a: Not always a large one. A short panel session and a brief survey of job holders can produce a defensible task list for a single role. The essential parts are a documented method, ratings of importance or criticality, and a clear link from tasks to what is trained and assessed.

DACUM: acronym for Developing a Curriculum; first developed in Canada in late 60s and early 70s; panel of experts, usually six to ten members; duties and tasks; typically two days face to face; foundation for competency-based training
